claim: Many species of plankton feeding on a limited variety of resources coexist, apparently flouting the competitive exclusion principle (CEP).
source: A long-standing puzzle lies in the paradox of the plankton: many species of plankton feeding on a limited variety of resources coexist, apparently flouting the competitive exclusion principle (CEP), which holds that the number of predator (consumer) species cannot exceed that of the resources at a steady state.
evidence: This is a statement about the paradox of plankton, which is established knowledge in ecology and is presented as the motivation for the study.

claim: The competitive exclusion principle holds that the number of predator (consumer) species cannot exceed that of the resources at a steady state.
source: A long-standing puzzle lies in the paradox of the plankton: many species of plankton feeding on a limited variety of resources coexist, apparently flouting the competitive exclusion principle (CEP), which holds that the number of predator (consumer) species cannot exceed that of the resources at a steady state.
evidence: This is a definition of CEP, which is established ecological theory.

claim: Intraspecific interference among consumers enables a plethora of consumer species to coexist at constant population densities with only one or a handful of resource species.
source: Here, we present a mechanistic model and demonstrate that intraspecific interference among the consumers enables a plethora of consumer species to coexist at constant population densities with only one or a handful of resource species.
evidence: This is the main finding of the study, supported by the modeling and simulation results presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: The facilitated biodiversity through intraspecific interference is resistant to stochasticity.
source: This facilitated biodiversity is resistant to stochasticity, either with the stochastic simulation algorithm or individual-based modeling.
evidence: This claim is supported by SSA and IBM simulation results shown in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: The model naturally explains classical experiments that invalidate the CEP.
source: Our model naturally explains the classical experiments that invalidate the CEP, quantitatively illustrates the universal S-shaped pattern of the rank-abundance curves across a wide range of ecological communities, and can be broadly used to resolve the mystery of biodiversity in many natural ecosystems.
evidence: This is supported by the comparison with experimental data from Ayala (1969) and Park (1954) shown in Figure 2D and E.

claim: The model quantitatively illustrates the universal S-shaped pattern of the rank-abundance curves across a wide range of ecological communities.
source: Our model naturally explains the classical experiments that invalidate the CEP, quantitatively illustrates the universal S-shaped pattern of the rank-abundance curves across a wide range of ecological communities, and can be broadly used to resolve the mystery of biodiversity in many natural ecosystems.
evidence: This is supported by the comparison with experimental data from multiple ecological communities shown in Figure 3C and D.

claim: In tropical forests, thousands of plant and vertebrate species coexist.
source: In tropical forests, thousands of plant and vertebrate species coexist (Hoorn et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Hoorn et al., 2010.

claim: Within a gram of soil, the number of microbial species is estimated to be 2000–18,000.
source: Within a gram of soil, the number of microbial species is estimated to be 2000–18,000 (Daniel, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Daniel, 2005.

claim: In the photic zone of the world ocean, there are roughly 150,000 eukaryotic plankton species.
source: In the photic zone of the world ocean, there are roughly 150,000 eukaryotic plankton species (de Vargas et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to de Vargas et al., 2015.

claim: Two species competing for a single type of resources cannot coexist at constant population densities.
source: A great challenge stems from the well-known competitive exclusion principle (CEP): two species competing for a single type of resources cannot coexist at constant population densities (Gause, 1934; Hardin, 1960), or generically, in the framework of consumer-resource models, the number of consumer species cannot exceed that of resources at a steady state (MacArthur and Levins, 1964; Levin, 1970; McGehee, 1977).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Gause, 1934 and Hardin, 1960.

claim: In the framework of consumer-resource models, the number of consumer species cannot exceed that of resources at a steady state.
source: A great challenge stems from the well-known competitive exclusion principle (CEP): two species competing for a single type of resources cannot coexist at constant population densities (Gause, 1934; Hardin, 1960), or generically, in the framework of consumer-resource models, the number of consumer species cannot exceed that of resources at a steady state (MacArthur and Levins, 1964; Levin, 1970; McGehee, 1977).
evidence: This is supported by citations to MacArthur and Levins, 1964; Levin, 1970; McGehee, 1977.

claim: A limited variety of resources supports hundreds or more coexisting species of phytoplankton in the paradox of plankton.
source: On the contrary, in the paradox of plankton, a limited variety of resources supports hundreds or more coexisting species of phytoplankton (Hutchinson, 1961).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Hutchinson, 1961.

claim: Various mechanisms have been put forward to overcome the limits set by CEP.
source: Ever since MacArthur and Levin proposed the classical mathematical proof for CEP in the 1960s (MacArthur and Levins, 1964), various mechanisms have been put forward to overcome the limits set by CEP (Chesson, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Chesson, 2000.

claim: Some mechanisms suggest that the system never approaches a steady state where the CEP applies, due to temporal variations, spatial heterogeneity, or species' self-organized dynamics.
source: Some suggest that the system never approaches a steady state where the CEP applies, due to temporal variations (Hutchinson, 1961; Levins, 1979), spatial heterogeneity (Levin, 1974), or species' self-organized dynamics (Koch, 1974; Huisman and Weissing, 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Predator interference is commonly described by the classical Beddington-DeAngelis (B-D) phenomenological model.
source: Predator interference is commonly described by the classical Beddington-DeAngelis (B-D) phenomenological model (Beddington, 1975; DeAngelis et al., 1975).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Beddington, 1975 and DeAngelis et al., 1975.

claim: Several studies have shown that intraspecific predator interference can break CEP and facilitate species coexistence through the application of the B-D model.
source: Through the application of the B-D model, several studies (Cantrell et al., 2004; Hsu et al., 2013) have shown that intraspecific predator interference can break CEP and facilitate species coexistence.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Cantrell et al., 2004 and Hsu et al., 2013.

claim: The functional response of the B-D model can be formally derived from a scenario solely involving chasing pairs without accounting for pairwise encounters among consumer individuals.
source: However, from a mechanistic perspective, the functional response of the B-D model can be formally derived from a scenario solely involving chasing pairs, representing the consumption process between consumers and resources, without accounting for pairwise encounters among consumer individuals (Wang and Liu, 2020; Huisman and De Boer, 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Wang and Liu, 2020 and Huisman and De Boer, 1997.

claim: The scenario involving only chasing pairs is subject to the constraint of CEP.
source: Disturbingly, it has been established that the scenario involving only chasing pairs is subject to the constraint of CEP (Wang and Liu, 2020), raising doubt regarding the validity of applying the B-D model to overcome the CEP.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Wang and Liu, 2020.

claim: The intraspecific interference among consumer individuals effectively constitutes a negative feedback loop.
source: The intraspecific interference among consumer individuals effectively constitutes a negative feedback loop, enabling a wide range of consumer species to coexist with only one or a few types of resources.
evidence: This is supported by the mathematical analysis and simulation results presented in the manuscript.

claim: The coexistence state facilitated by intraspecific interference is resistant to stochasticity and can be realized in practice.
source: The coexistence state is resistant to stochasticity and can hence be realized in practice.
evidence: This is supported by SSA and IBM simulation results.

claim: The model naturally explains species coexistence in classical experiments that invalidate CEP by Ayala (1969) and Park (1954).
source: In particular, it naturally explains species coexistence in classical experiments that invalidate CEP (Ayala, 1969; Park, 1954) and quantitatively illustrates the S-shaped pattern of the rank-abundance curves in an extensive spectrum of ecological communities, ranging from the communities of ocean plankton worldwide (Fuhrman et al., 2008; Ser-Giacomi et al., 2018), tropical river fishes from Argentina (Cody and Smallwood, 1996), forest bats of Trinidad (Clarke et al., 2005), rainforest trees (Hubbell, 2001), birds (Terborgh et al., 1990; Martínez et al., 2023), butterflies (De Vries, 1997) in Amazonia, to those of desert bees (Hubbell, 2001) in Utah and lizards from South Australia (Cody and Smallwood, 1996).
evidence: This is supported by comparison with experimental data shown in Figure 2D and E.

claim: The model quantitatively illustrates the S-shaped pattern of the rank-abundance curves in ocean plankton communities worldwide.
source: In particular, it naturally explains species coexistence in classical experiments that invalidate CEP (Ayala, 1969; Park, 1954) and quantitatively illustrates the S-shaped pattern of the rank-abundance curves in an extensive spectrum of ecological communities, ranging from the communities of ocean plankton worldwide (Fuhrman et al., 2008; Ser-Giacomi et al., 2018), tropical river fishes from Argentina (Cody and Smallwood, 1996), forest bats of Trinidad (Clarke et al., 2005), rainforest trees (Hubbell, 2001), birds (Terborgh et al., 1990; Martínez et al., 2023), butterflies (De Vries, 1997) in Amazonia, to those of desert bees (Hubbell, 2001) in Utah and lizards from South Australia (Cody and Smallwood, 1996).
evidence: This is supported by comparison with experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: In the scenario involving only chasing pairs, consumer species cannot coexist at a steady state except for special parameter settings.
source: In the scenario involving only chasing pairs, consumer species cannot coexist at a steady state except for special parameter settings (sets of measure zero) (Wang and Liu, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Wang and Liu, 2020 and illustrated in Figure 1C and F.

claim: In the scenario involving chasing pairs and interspecific interference, the fixed point for species coexistence is unstable.
source: However, this fixed point is unstable (see Figure 1G and Appendix 1—figure 3D, F), and thus one of the consumer species is doomed to extinction (see Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 1G and simulation results in Figure 1D.

claim: In the scenario involving chasing pairs and intraspecific interference, two consumer species may stably coexist at a steady state with only one type of resources, which breaks CEP.
source: Indeed, this naturally happens, and encouragingly the fixed point can be stable. Therefore, two consumer species may stably coexist at a steady state with only one type of resources, which obviously breaks CEP (see Figure 1E and Appendix 1—figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by the analysis and simulation results shown in Figure 1E and H.

claim: The coexisting state in the scenario with intraspecific interference is globally attractive.
source: In fact, the coexisting state is globally attractive (see Appendix 1—figure 4A), and there exists a non-zero volume of parameter space where the two consumer species stably coexist at constant population densities (see Appendix 1—figure 4B, C), demonstrating that the violation of CEP does not depend on special parameter settings.
evidence: This is supported by simulation results shown in Appendix 1—figure 4A.

claim: There exists a non-zero volume of parameter space where two consumer species stably coexist at constant population densities.
source: In fact, the coexisting state is globally attractive (see Appendix 1—figure 4A), and there exists a non-zero volume of parameter space where the two consumer species stably coexist at constant population densities (see Appendix 1—figure 4B, C), demonstrating that the violation of CEP does not depend on special parameter settings.
evidence: This is supported by simulation results shown in Appendix 1—figure 4B, C.

claim: The violation of CEP through intraspecific interference does not depend on special parameter settings.
source: In fact, the coexisting state is globally attractive (see Appendix 1—figure 4A), and there exists a non-zero volume of parameter space where the two consumer species stably coexist at constant population densities (see Appendix 1—figure 4B, C), demonstrating that the violation of CEP does not depend on special parameter settings.
evidence: This is supported by the analysis of parameter space shown in Appendix 1—figure 4B, C.

claim: Two notable cases of oscillating coexistence turn into species extinction when stochasticity is introduced.
source: Consistent with this, we observe that two notable cases of oscillating coexistence (Koch, 1974; Huisman and Weissing, 1999) turn into species extinction when stochasticity is introduced (see Appendix 1—figure 6A, B), where we simulate the models with stochastic simulation algorithm (SSA; Gillespie, 2007) and adopt the same parameters as those in the original references (Koch, 1974; Huisman and Weissing, 1999).
evidence: This is supported by SSA simulation results shown in Appendix 1—figure 6A, B.

claim: In the scenario involving chasing pairs and intraspecific interference, species may coexist indefinitely in the SSA simulations.
source: In the scenario involving chasing pairs and intraspecific interference, species may coexist indefinitely in the SSA simulations (see Figure 2A and Appendix 1—figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by SSA simulation results shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The parameter region for species coexistence in the scenario with intraspecific interference is rather similar between the SSA and ODEs studies.
source: In fact, the parameter region for species coexistence in this scenario is rather similar between the SSA and ODEs studies (see Appendix 1—figure 6C, D).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of simulation results shown in Appendix 1—figure 6C, D.

claim: In the scenario involving chasing pairs and intraspecific interference, two consumer species coexist for long with only one type of resources in the IBM simulations.
source: In the scenario involving chasing pairs and intraspecific interference, two consumer species coexist for long with only one type of resources in the IBM simulations (see Figure 2B and C).
evidence: This is supported by IBM simulation results shown in Figure 2B and C.

claim: Intraspecific interference robustly promotes species coexistence when stochasticity is considered.
source: Together with the SSA simulation studies, it is obvious that intraspecific interference still robustly promotes species coexistence when stochasticity is considered.
evidence: This is supported by SSA and IBM simulation results shown in Figure 2.

claim: In Ayala's experiment, two Drosophila species coexisted with one type of resources within a laboratory bottle.
source: In practice, two classical studies (Ayala, 1969; Park, 1954) reported that, in their respective laboratory systems, two species of insects coexisted for roughly years or more with only one type of resources.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Ayala, 1969.

claim: In Park's experiment, two Tribolium species coexisted for 2 years with one type of food (flour) within a lab.
source: In practice, two classical studies (Ayala, 1969; Park, 1954) reported that, in their respective laboratory systems, two species of insects coexisted for roughly years or more with only one type of resources.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Park, 1954.

claim: The two experiments by Ayala (1969) and Park (1954) are incompatible with CEP.
source: Evidently, these two experiments (Ayala, 1969; Park, 1954) are incompatible with CEP, while factors such as temporal variations, spatial heterogeneity, cross-feeding, etc. are clearly not involved in such systems.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental results and the definition of CEP.

claim: Intraspecific fighting is prevalent among insects.
source: As intraspecific fighting is prevalent among insects (Boomsma et al., 2005; Dankert et al., 2009; Chen et al., 2002), we apply the model involving chasing pairs and intraspecific interference to simulate the two systems.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Boomsma et al., 2005; Dankert et al., 2009; Chen et al., 2002.

claim: The SSA results show good consistency with the experiments by Ayala (1969) and Park (1954).
source: Overall, our SSA results show good consistency with those of the experiments (see Figure 2D and E and Appendix 1—figure 7).
evidence: This is supported by comparison with experimental data shown in Figure 2D and E.

claim: The fluctuations in experimental time series can be mainly accounted by stochasticity.
source: The fluctuations in experimental time series can be mainly accounted by stochasticity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison between SSA simulations and experimental data.

claim: The number of consumer species in long-term coexistence can be up to hundreds or more.
source: The number of consumer species in long-term coexistence can be up to hundreds or more (see Figure 3 and Appendix 1—figure 8).
evidence: This is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 3 and Appendix 1—figure 8.

claim: The analytical steady-state solutions are highly consistent with the numerical results.
source: The analytical steady-state solutions are highly consistent with the numerical results (see Figure 1E and Appendix 1—figure 3H, I) and can even quantitatively predict the coexistence region of the parameter space (see Appendix 1—figure 3I).
evidence: This is supported by comparison between analytical and numerical results shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The analytical solutions can quantitatively predict the coexistence region of the parameter space.
source: The analytical steady-state solutions are highly consistent with the numerical results (see Figure 1E and Appendix 1—figure 3H, I) and can even quantitatively predict the coexistence region of the parameter space (see Appendix 1—figure 3I).
evidence: This is supported by comparison shown in Appendix 1—figure 3I.

claim: The species' rank-abundance curves follow a universal S-shaped pattern in the linear-log plot across a broad spectrum of ecological communities.
source: As mentioned above, a prominent feature of biodiversity is that the species' rank-abundance curves follow a universal S-shaped pattern in the linear-log plot across a broad spectrum of ecological communities (Fuhrman et al., 2008; Ser-Giacomi et al., 2018; Cody and Smallwood, 1996; Terborgh et al., 1990; Martínez et al., 2023; Clarke et al., 2005; Hubbell, 2001; De Vries, 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: The S-shaped pattern was mostly explained by the neutral theory, which requires special parameter settings that all consumer species share identical fitness.
source: Previously, this pattern was mostly explained by the neutral theory (Hubbell, 2001), which requires special parameter settings that all consumer species share identical fitness.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Hubbell, 2001.

claim: The rank-abundance curves obtained from the long-term coexisting state of both the ODEs and SSA simulation studies agree quantitatively with those of experiments.
source: For a broad array of the ecological communities, the rank-abundance curves obtained from the long-term coexisting state of both the ODEs and SSA simulation studies agree quantitatively with those of experiments (see Figure 3C and D and Appendix 1—figures 8–14), sharing roughly equal Shannon entropies and mostly being regarded as identical distributions in the Kolmogorov-Smirnov (K-S) statistical test (with a significance threshold of 0.05).
evidence: This is supported by comparison with experimental data shown in Figure 3C and D.

claim: The simulation results and experimental data share roughly equal Shannon entropies.
source: For a broad array of the ecological communities, the rank-abundance curves obtained from the long-term coexisting state of both the ODEs and SSA simulation studies agree quantitatively with those of experiments (see Figure 3C and D and Appendix 1—figures 8–14), sharing roughly equal Shannon entropies and mostly being regarded as identical distributions in the Kolmogorov-Smirnov (K-S) statistical test (with a significance threshold of 0.05).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the simulation and experimental data.

claim: The simulation results and experimental data are mostly regarded as identical distributions in the Kolmogorov-Smirnov (K-S) statistical test.
source: For a broad array of the ecological communities, the rank-abundance curves obtained from the long-term coexisting state of both the ODEs and SSA simulation studies agree quantitatively with those of experiments (see Figure 3C and D and Appendix 1—figures 8–14), sharing roughly equal Shannon entropies and mostly being regarded as identical distributions in the Kolmogorov-Smirnov (K-S) statistical test (with a significance threshold of 0.05).
evidence: This is supported by K-S test results with p-values reported in Figure 3.

claim: There is a noticeable discrepancy between the experimental data and SSA studies in terms of the species' absolute abundances.
source: Still, there is a noticeable discrepancy between the experimental data and SSA studies in terms of the species' absolute abundances (e.g. see Appendix 1—figure 8C): those with experimental abundances less than 10 tend to be extinct in the SSA simulations.
evidence: This is observed in the comparison shown in Appendix 1—figure 8C.

claim: Species with experimental abundances less than 10 tend to be extinct in the SSA simulations.
source: Still, there is a noticeable discrepancy between the experimental data and SSA studies in terms of the species' absolute abundances (e.g. see Appendix 1—figure 8C): those with experimental abundances less than 10 tend to be extinct in the SSA simulations.
evidence: This is observed in the SSA simulation results.

claim: The recorded individuals in an experimental sample are just a tiny portion of that in the real ecological system.
source: This is due to the fact that the recorded individuals in an experimental sample are just a tiny portion of that in the real ecological system, whereas the species population size in a natural community is certainly much larger than 10.
evidence: This is an inference based on ecological knowledge.

claim: The species population size in a natural community is certainly much larger than 10.
source: This is due to the fact that the recorded individuals in an experimental sample are just a tiny portion of that in the real ecological system, whereas the species population size in a natural community is certainly much larger than 10.
evidence: This is based on ecological knowledge.

claim: The functional response of the B-D model involving intraspecific interference can be formally derived from the scenario involving only chasing pairs without consideration of pairwise encounters between consumer individuals.
source: In fact, predator interference has been introduced long ago by the classical B-D phenomenological model (Beddington, 1975; DeAngelis et al., 1975). However, the functional response of the B-D model involving intraspecific interference can be formally derived from the scenario involving only chasing pairs without consideration of pairwise encounters between consumer individuals (Wang and Liu, 2020; Huisman and De Boer, 1997; see Equations S8a and S24a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Wang and Liu, 2020 and Huisman and De Boer, 1997.

claim: It is questionable regarding the validity of applying the B-D model to break CEP.
source: Therefore, it is questionable regarding the validity of applying the B-D model to break CEP (Cantrell et al., 2004; Hsu et al., 2013).
evidence: This is an inference based on the analysis that the B-D model can be derived from a scenario subject to CEP.

claim: The B-D model corresponds to a special case of the mechanistic model without the escape rate.
source: From a mechanistic perspective, we resolve these issues and show that the B-D model corresponds to a special case of our mechanistic model yet without the escape rate (see Appendix 1—figure 2 and Appendix 3 for details).
evidence: This is supported by the mathematical analysis shown in Appendix 1—figure 2 and Appendix 3.

claim: The model is broadly applicable to explain biodiversity in many ecosystems.
source: Our model is broadly applicable to explain biodiversity in many ecosystems.
evidence: This is supported by the successful application to multiple ecological communities shown in Figure 3.

claim: In microbial systems, complex interactions are commonly involved.
source: In microbial systems, complex interactions are commonly involved (Goyal and Maslov, 2018; Goldford et al., 2018; Hu et al., 2022), and species' preference for food is shaped by the evolutionary course and environmental history (Wang et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Species' preference for food is shaped by the evolutionary course and environmental history.
source: In microbial systems, complex interactions are commonly involved (Goyal and Maslov, 2018; Goldford et al., 2018; Hu et al., 2022), and species' preference for food is shaped by the evolutionary course and environmental history (Wang et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Wang et al., 2019.

claim: It is highly challenging to fully explain how organisms evolve and maintain biodiversity in diverse ecosystems.
source: It is still highly challenging to fully explain how organisms evolve and maintain biodiversity in diverse ecosystems.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in ecology.

claim: The mortality rates of consumer species in the model simulations follow a Gaussian distribution where the coefficient of variation was taken around 0.3.
source: In each model system, the mortality rates of consumer species follow a Gaussian distribution where the coefficient of variation was taken around 0.3 (Menon et al., 2003; see Appendix 9 for details).
evidence: This is a parameter setting for the simulations, supported by a citation to Menon et al., 2003.
